newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe sees fresh foreign equity flows.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe sees fresh foreign equity flows.

text.p: Zimbabwe is set to attract fresh flows of foreign investment after the government increased the level of permitted foreign shareholdings, share market officials and analysts said on Thursday.

By raising the amount of equity foreigners were allowed to buy in a company on the Zimbabwe Stock Exchange (ZSE), the government was signalling its commitment to open up the country's economy to foreign investment.
"It's very positive and will result in additional foreign investor inflows," Savvas Kyriakides, managing director of stock and economic analysts Dataworld, told Reuters.
Zimbabwe's central Reserve Bank on Wednesday raised to 40 percent from 35 percent the amount of equity foreigners are allowed to buy in a Zimbabwean company.

"As part of ongoing efforts to improve the investment climate, the present limit of 35 percent foreign investor participation on the Zimbabwe Stock Exchange is raised, with immediate effect, to 40 percent," Reserve Bank governor Leonard Tsumba said in a statement released late Wednesday.

In measures previously urged by brokers and market analysts to stimulate growth on the local bourse, Tsumba also said a single investor could now own up to 10 percent of the equity of a listed company, compared with five percent previously.

"The government is moving in the right direction, that it wants foreign investment in the stock market. It sends out the right signals to the foreign investor that the government is opening up the economy," said ZSE deputy chairman Trudy Cashell.
She said the measures could see a return of foreign buying in some companies which had reached the 35 percent limit.

The southern African country first opened up its stock market to foreign investors in May 1993 under Western-backed economic reforms it adopted in 1991. Since then, the market has attracted net foreign investment inflows amounting to U.S.$140 million.

Cashell and some brokers said they expected Wednesday's measures to propel the local bourse higher, anchoring its place as one of the world's top emerging market performers, a tag it has boasted for the past three years.

The market is already on a bull-run fuelled by prospects of lower interest rates after the Reserve Bank last month cut its key rediscount rate to 27.5 percent from 29.5 percent after a fall in annual inflation to 22 percent in July from 28 percent in January.

The ZSE's key industrial index has been scaling new levels daily from last week. On Wednesday, it surged through the psychological 6,000 barrier after soaring 247.93 points, its biggest ever one-day gain, to close at a record high of 6,165.26.

Brokers said the market was still shrugging off concerns about the rapid rate of money supply growth -- which Tsumba said remained stubbornly high at above 22 percent -- and the financial impact of a two-week strike by civil servants which paralysed essential social services.
